source_text: Apostolus quippe Ioannes cum ad virtutum omnium fastigium provocaret fideles, et studium sanctitatis ad altitudinem dominicae conversationis extenderet, ad compendium, mundi totius nomine universa praesentium bonorum et iucunditatum irritamenta concludens: Nolite - inquit - diligere mundum, neque ea quae in mundo sunt. Si quis diligit mundum, non est caritas Patris in eo; quoniam omne quod est in mundo, concupiscentia carnis, et concupiscentia oculorum est, et superbia vitae; quae non est ex Patre, sed ex mundo est; et mundus transit, et concupiscentia eius; qui autem facit voluntatem Dei, manet in aeternum [n32] . Quantum ad superficiem verborum respicit, odium omnibus indicit elementis, et mundum et cuncta quae in mundo sunt, non esse ex Patre, neque diligi debere denuntiat.
pass_a_gloss: The Apostle John, indeed, when he was calling the faithful to the summit of all virtues, and was stretching the zeal of holiness to the height of the Lord's way of life, for brevity, enclosing by the name of the whole world all the irritants of present goods and delights: Do not — he says — love the world, nor those things which are in the world. If anyone loves the world, the charity of the Father is not in him; because everything that is in the world is the desire of the flesh, and the desire of the eyes, and the pride of life; which is not from the Father, but is from the world; and the world passes, and its desire; but he who does the will of God remains forever. As far as it looks to the surface of the words, he declares hatred on all the elements, and denounces that the world and all things which are in the world are not from the Father, nor ought to be loved.

lemmas.lexica: LS concupiscentia=eager desire; Blaise Christian usage often sexual desire vs nuptiae
LS voluntas=will, wish; Blaise moral will

pass_b_english: For the apostle John was urging the faithful toward the summit of every virtue and stretching their pursuit of holiness to the height of the Lord’s manner of life. To be brief, he embraced under the name of the whole world every attraction of present goods and pleasures: “Do not love the world or the things in the world. If anyone loves the world, the Father’s love is not in him, because everything in the world is the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and the pride of life, which is not from the Father but from the world. The world passes away, and its desire; but whoever does God’s will remains forever” (1 John 2:15–17). If we look only at the surface of the words, he commands hatred of all the elements and declares that the world and everything in it are not from the Father and should not be loved.

choices.why: Julian distinguishes nuptiae from concupiscentia; do not flatten to 'lust' as a nature-sin substance.
Julian's definition of sin is an act of will. Keep 'will' rather than later 'free will' system language unless liberum arbitrium is present.
Paul in Julian's citations; keep Apostle not 'Paul' unless Paulus is written.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded.

bible_refs.note: From Pass B Scripture tagging; wording follows Julian's Latin, not a modern Bible.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Opus imperfectum contra Iulianum); Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
